newsitem.title: USA: Tracking new soybean through food chain a tough task.
newsitem.headline: Tracking new soybean through food chain a tough task.

text.p: Tracking a soybean's path from the field through the processing plant and into hundreds of processed foods is virtually impossible, industry experts say.
But that is what some consumer groups are asking in order to ensure that food products made from new genetically altered soybeans can be identified and carry consumer-advice labels.
"It's not like a carrot," said Karen Marshall, a spokeswoman for Monsanto Co. "They (soybean products) are in candy bars, cookies, crackers. It's virtually everywhere."
At issue in this latest battle between some consumer groups and food companies is a new soybean developed by Monsanto that has been genetically altered to resist the potent herbicide Roundup.

A large number of other organisations both in the United States and overseas have approved the soybean for use in foods, and they say scientific tests have proven it is no different from conventional soybeans.
"They look like, taste like and process like soybeans because they are soybeans," said David Erickson, president of the American Soybean Association, which respresents U.S. soybean farmers.
The new soybeans are being harvested for the first time this year from nearly 1 million acres. But usage is forecast to increase tenfold next year.

Tracking soybeans for the purposes of labeling them for human consumption is nearly impossible. Soybeans from different fields are frequently mixed by farmers and are mixed again at grain elevators and again at points throughout the marketing chain.
Soybean meal and oil are the two main products made from soybeans. About 80 percent of the soybean is made into soymeal and the balance into soyoil.
Soybean oil is used in cooking oil, margarine, mayonnaise, salad oils, and processed foods. Industrial uses include newpaper ink, plastics, and adhesives.
Soymeal is mainly used as a livestock feed, but it also has a growing use in human foods.

At a press conference Monday, the Pure Food Campaign, which says it represents consumer, farm and environmental interests, announced a boycott against several food companies, claiming the companies rejected the group's request not to use altered soybeans or to label products made from them.
A survey of U.S. grain dealers indicates most will handle the altered soybeans the same as conventional ones.
"I think it will be very difficult for the market to find a way to sort GMO's (genetically modified organisms)," said one exporter.

Some grain dealers said they are discussing a plan to offer supplies of non-genetically altered soybeans, but the plan may rely largely on a farmer's word whether the soybeans are from conventional seed.

"The calls for labeling are begging the question because that presumes there is some difference ... and that just isn't true," said Sheldon Hauch, president of the National Oilseed Processors Association, which represents soybean processing companies.
